_meta.model: claude-sonnet-4-6 (MODELS.SMART), 1 endpoint (/signal-vs-noise, fans out to 2 parallel calls merged server-side)
_meta.baseline_commit: signalvsnoise-v8 (owner-supplied researched rebuild: web-search pre-pass + cited synthesis)
_meta.v5_note: v4's regex (CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE) was verb-conjugation-specific ('evidence shows/suggests/supports') and missed 12 of 13 real violations in the very next live test, a parenting/screen-time topic: 'the evidence tends to show,' 'observational research,' 'reviews of homework research... broadly recognized in ... literature,' 'researchers argue,' 'is associated with,' 'historically,' 'documented,' 'the evidence on X is Y.' Narrow verb-matching does not generalize across the many ways a model phrases 'I reviewed a body of evidence' — v5's list is now broad WORD/PHRASE matching (evidence/research + up to 3 words + a wide verb set, bare 'literature'/'historically'/'documented'/'associated with', etc.), verified against all 13 new violations plus 7 legitimate ALLOWED sentences (0 false positives, 0 false negatives) before shipping. ARCHITECTURE CHANGE: enforcement moved from a whole-CALL regenerate (v4) to PER-FIELD regenerate (v5) — enforceClaimModeFields()/regenerateField()/setAtPath() rewrite only the flagged sentence (cheap, MODELS.FAST, no JSON schema to fill), preserving everything the model got right instead of risking a whole-half regenerate trading one violation for a different one elsewhere. A field that still fails after its one regeneration attempt is left as-is and the EXISTING structural clean()-filter (unchanged) drops the enclosing item, same fallback as before. NEW: a traceability/scope-creep guard (rule 21 extended + 5 new outputGuard entries) — the same live test also introduced 'free-range parenting' and invented 'the core of free-range parenting' as a model-generated definition, neither of which the visitor raised (visitor supplied only screen time, tiger vs. free-range as a *label pair*, and homework — not a definition of any of them). Rule 21 now states an explicit traceability test (A: a supplied claim, B: a necessary distinction, C: an examined source — if none apply, don't write it). Also reinforced: rule 26 (new) — the_signal doesn't need one item per noise item, don't insert an unprompted epistemic lesson (e.g. 'before-and-after comparisons') the visitor didn't raise, don't invent an individual child/person to apply a population claim to (that belongs in what_general_claims_cant_decide, not the general bottom line). UI: a 'CLAIM ANALYSIS' mode badge with a tooltip now renders under ANALYZING (source_analysis/verified_research labels are unreachable today — this tool performs no live retrieval — and are not yet built; add them only if that capability is ever added). Catalog copy (src/data/tools.js description/seoDescription/primer.get) and svn_tagline reworded away from 'stronger evidence'/'genuinely unsettled' framing that implied the tool always has access to an evidence base, per the same principle as SOURCE MODE. Live-tested against the exact parenting/screen-time/homework scenario (0 banned-phrase hits, 0 field-fix regenerations needed — the strengthened prompt got it right without needing the backstop this time; the backstop's correctness was verified separately via 20 unit test cases against the regex directly). DO NOT revert to whole-call regeneration or narrow the banned-phrase list back to verb-conjugation matching — both were the specific gaps this pass closed.
_meta.v4_note: A THIRD 'final corrections' pass, same day as v3, found the identical literature-review-voice failure in a domain not yet tested — finance ('persistent tracking of fund returns... across multiple markets and asset classes,' 'the evidence covers funds that survived long enough to be measured,' a fabricated survivorship-bias limitation for a dataset never examined). Three prompt-only passes had not fully suppressed this, so v4 adds what they didn't have: a deterministic, ENGLISH-ONLY code-level backstop (see signal-vs-noise.js's CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE / findBannedPhrase / callClaimModeChecked) — every prose field is scanned against a fixed phrase list, a violating half is regenerated once with the exact offending phrase quoted back at it, and any array item that still violates after that is silently dropped rather than shown. The prompt still tries hard to get it right the first time (extensive new PERSONALITY rules, worked BAD/GOOD examples for the fee/valuation/real-estate/survivorship/professional-referral/ranking-against-unnamed-alternatives failures) — the regex is the guarantee, not a replacement for it. SCHEMA CHANGE: genuinely_debated (with nullable what_supports_one_view/another_view, introduced in v3) is REMOVED entirely and replaced by two separate top-level arrays: still_worth_verifying[] ({question, why_it_matters, what_would_help} — a genuinely unresolved GENERAL empirical question, never a fabricated two-sided debate) and what_general_claims_cant_decide[] (plain strings — person-specific questions a general analysis can never resolve, e.g. 'whether direct real estate fits your actual situation'). v3's null-views mechanism for person-dependent questions is superseded by this split, not extended. Response also gains analysis_mode ('claim_analysis', hard-locked in code, not model-self-reported) and sources_examined (always [] today — no source-paste feature exists). Caps changed: the_signal 4->3, still_worth_verifying capped at 2 (was genuinely_debated at 3), what_general_claims_cant_decide capped at 3, the_bottom_line.what_would_change_the_answer 2->3. i18n: svn_nuance reworded 'Limits:' -> "What it doesn't establish:"; svn_debated_header reworded 'Still Unsettled' -> 'Still Worth Verifying'; new keys svn_verify_why/svn_verify_would_help/svn_cant_decide_header; svn_one_view/svn_another_view/svn_why_unsettled are now orphaned (left in the locale files, no longer referenced in JSX — the two-sided-debate UI was removed, not relabeled). outputGuard.prohibit grew from 28 to 37 entries. DO NOT reverse the schema split or the code-level regex backstop — three prompt-only passes already proved insufficient on their own.
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden signal-vs-noise). v2 (2026-09-09) fixed the health-domain instances of the tool implying a literature review it never performed. v3 (2026-09-10) fixed the SAME failure mode recurring in a non-health (career/labor) domain — 'wage data shows,' an invented MBA-recruiting market map, an invented causal mechanism for job-switching pay, a strawmanned 'follow your passion' critique, an extra unrequested career-advice claim, two noise_type mislabels, an unsupported publicity/selection-bias claim used to rebut an overclaim with another overclaim, debate-club phrasing, and a STILL UNSETTLED section forced into a two-sided-evidence shape it didn't have for a person-dependent question. v4 (same day) is documented in v4_note above. v5 (2026-09-10) is documented in v5_note above. v6 (2026-09-10) is documented in v6_note above.
_meta.prior_notes: v2 (2026-09-09) was a full owner-supplied rewrite: the v1 tool asserted "real consensus," named specific actors as "generating noise," and invoked specific research designs, biomarkers, genetic variants, and validation findings from memory as though it had performed a sourced evidence review — exactly the authority the tool was never in a position to claim. Schema changed completely from v1 (why_this_field_is_noisy -> framing; the_signal.items[].why_we_know_this -> basis; .the_nuance -> limits; genuinely_debated[].side_a/side_b -> what_supports_one_view/what_supports_another_view (later removed entirely in v4); the_noise[] gained what_the_evidence_supports_instead alongside renamed what_went_wrong (was the_problem); the_bottom_line's three single-string fields became three arrays; sources_of_noise[].actor/incentive/how_to_spot_it -> source_type/how_it_distorts/how_to_recognize_it, no longer naming an accused actor). Guards added that pass: NO_QUOTE_RULE, router.outputStandard='v2' + outputGuard, and a post-guard structural validation pass (see code comment: the guard mutates its argument in place and its repair pass can leave a field incomplete despite instructions not to).
_meta.v6_note: A FOURTH 'final corrections' pass, sleep domain, confirmed the deterministic claim_analysis mode switch (v4) had finally killed the fake-literature-review voice, but found a narrower, different failure: unlabeled empirical premises imported from memory that never use evidence-provenance wording at all, so CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE cannot catch them ('most adults need roughly 7-9 hours', 'light exposure is one input to the body's circadian timing system', 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness'), plus a logical non-sequitur reasoning backward from a metaphor's usefulness to a fact about the thing it describes ('if a single recovery night fully erased all sleep debt, the metaphor wouldn't be useful'), plus a bottom line that broke back into sleep/parenting/finance guidance and invented personal context nobody supplied in what_would_change_the_answer. FIX (prompt-level, not regex — this class of error has no stable lexical marker a regex can key on): new rule 27 ('WHAT AUTHORIZES THIS SENTENCE?') gives the model an explicit 3-way test before writing any factual sentence — A. USER_CLAIM (the visitor supplied it), B. LOGIC (follows from the claim's own structure, no empirical finding needed), C. LABELED_BACKGROUND (genuinely ordinary vocabulary-only background, used sparingly, never the central empirical answer) — rewrite or remove if none apply. New rule 28 fixes the metaphor non-sequitur (critique what a metaphor fails to establish, never reason backward from 'what would make it useful'). New rule 29 locks the bottom line to summarizing the claim analysis only, and reserves personal-situation language in what_would_change_the_answer for when the visitor actually supplied enough personal context to identify a real gap. NORTH STAR gained a prepended 3-line frame: use knowledge to understand the claim, logic to test it, evidence to settle it. TRAP HIT AND FIXED DURING THIS PASS: the rule 27/29 illustrative BAD examples quoted the exact attractor phrase 'additional sleep after restriction can reduce sleepiness' TWICE, verbatim — live testing showed the model echoing that near-verbatim phrase straight into output (a known trap: worked BAD-example text gets copied rather than avoided, see deftbrain-voice-prompt-traps memory). Fixed by rewriting both examples to describe the ERROR PATTERN in the abstract (no specific number, no specific mechanism, no specific magnitude-of-benefit claim to copy) plus an explicit 'this is illustrating a pattern, not a script — a close paraphrase is the same violation' instruction. Verified 0 banned-phrase / 0 attractor-phrase hits across 3 consecutive live regenerations of the exact sleep scenario after the reword (the run before the reword produced the attractor phrase; the runs after did not). UI: added a visible 'No outside sources reviewed' sub-label beside the CLAIM ANALYSIS badge (the existing badge only had it in a hover tooltip, poor discoverability) and a 'Research These Claims' disclosure at the end of results, built from still_worth_verifying (falling back to what_would_change_the_answer) with one external search-engine link per open question — pure frontend, no new backend capability. This is deliberately NOT a live-retrieval / verified-research mode: the tool has no wired search or fetch capability, and building real retrieval is an infrastructure decision (external dependency, cost per request, latency, reliability) flagged to the owner rather than silently built or silently dropped, same position as the v5 note. i18n: svn_honest_uncertainty relabeled '? What Could Change the Answer' -> '? What Would Help' across all 13 languages (claim-analysis mode is never about the visitor's personal situation, so the more evidence-focused label is now the default; a personalized 'what could change the answer' framing would need a genuinely supplied personal-context case, which this tool does not yet branch on). New keys: svn_no_sources_reviewed, svn_research_these_claims, svn_research_intro, svn_search_this (13 languages each). DO NOT re-quote a specific number, mechanism, or magnitude figure in rule 27/28/29's illustrative examples — describe the pattern, never the sentence.
_meta.v7_note: V7 replaces 'regex + one regen' with a five-stage CLAIM ANALYSIS VALIDATION PIPELINE in the route: (1) CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, demoted to cheap first-pass detection; (2) a SEMANTIC EMPIRICAL-RESOLUTION CHECK — a judged call asking ONE narrow question per field (does this text assert or rely on a real-world proposition that was not supplied, not sourced in this run, and materially helps decide the claim? hedges do not convert FAIL to PASS); (3) one per-field REWRITE with the owner's exact rewrite prompt; (4) REVALIDATE the rewrite alone (regex + judge, batch size 1); (5) a fixed, LOCALIZED SAFE FALLBACK per field type (13 languages, in CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS) — never a second regeneration, because a validator/regenerator loop is exactly how the model finds new vocabulary for the same assertion. Fields with no fallback (a signal item's claim, a still_worth_verifying question, a sources_of_noise field, a person-specific item) are blanked so the structural filter drops the item. 5b: a signal item whose basis fell back gets its CLAIM re-judged alone and dropped unless it passes — a fixed basis under an unlicensed claim would lend it the very logical veneer the pipeline removes. WHY: five consecutive prompt-only passes (tool rules 14/27-29, then two rounds of the global epistemics contract) all failed the same live nutrition test the same way — the model stopped saying 'research shows' and started stating bare or hedged premises ('hormones regulate appetite and energy expenditure', 'meal timing may interact with circadian rhythms', 'intermittent fasting is a workable structure for some people'), or laundering them through 'this follows from the accounting relationship'. No lexical marker exists for that; a phrase list structurally cannot see it. MEASURED DURING BUILD: (a) judge recall collapses with batch size — one call over all 48 fields flagged 3 and missed the two plainest violations; the same two fields alone were both flagged in 1.7s — hence SEMANTIC_BATCH_SIZE=6, parallel; (b) the judge is consistent (3/3) on what it flags but neighborhood-sensitive, hence two offset passes unioned at stage 2; (c) the judge itself got laundered by 'this follows from the structure...' framing until told to judge every sentence on its own. Standalone replay of a leaked response through the finished pipeline: semantic=9 rewritten=6 fallback=2 blanked=1, and a fresh judge pass over the result found the flagship leaks gone. Live: 4 consecutive runs, fallbacks firing 1-5 times per run, route time ~60s (parallel judge calls; +10-20s vs v6). COST: roughly 20-35 small MODELS.SMART calls per request on a leaky response — a deliberate trade for a tool whose entire promise is this discipline. GOLDEN: schema unchanged; sources_of_noise and what_general_claims_cant_decide are now optionalSections on every case because the pipeline legitimately empties them (their fields have no fallback text, so a flagged item drops). DO NOT: collapse the judge back to one big batch; add a second regeneration attempt; let a rewrite through when its recheck was unavailable; give sources_of_noise/still_worth_verifying fields a fallback (they'd become filler).
_meta.v7_1_note: V7.1 (same day): SEMANTIC_CHECK_SYSTEM is now the owner's supplied validation prompt (PASS only if every substantive claim is visitor-supplied or logical analysis needing no extra real-world premise; FAIL on remembered knowledge, unsupplied examples, 'unestablished then asserted anyway', hedge-disguised claims, conclusions not established by validated material; counterfactual key test), wrapped in the batch/JSON contract plus a CLARIFICATIONS block. Measured: as written it over-flagged the tool's own correct output (flagged 'is an empirical question this analysis cannot settle'; one live run blanked the whole Signal section). Restoring the owner's earlier 'ignore statements that merely define / analyze wording / identify missing info / say evidence is needed' list fixed that (replay: blanked 1 -> 0, signal item kept). Live cost with the final prompt on the nutrition scenario: 12 fallbacks in one run (5/8 bottom-line items boilerplate) — the rule applied faithfully; boilerplate density is the owner's call, documented in the tool notes. Flagship BAD sentences ('hormonal factors operate within the energy-balance relationship', 'not competing explanations — they interact') added verbatim to MUST-fail examples after the solo re-judge passed one of them once.
_meta.v7_2_note: V7.2 (same day): fallback PRESENTATION only, judge untouched. (1) bottom_line fallback split into per-list wording takeaway/skeptical/would_help, each with a _many variant, 13 languages. (2) optional sub-fields (kernel_of_truth, signal limits) are OMITTED on failure (null) instead of replaced — UI renders them only when present. (3) collapseBottomLineFallbacks: within each bottom-line list, survivors untouched, all fallback items fold into at most one bullet placed last (singular wording for one failure, _many for several) — a variable-length Bottom Line, per DEFTBRAIN_OUTPUT_STANDARD_V2's preference for omission over redundant completeness. Bug caught by the fallback unit test before shipping: English would_help fallbacks began 'Evidence about…', matching CLAIM_MODE_BANNED_RE, so the structural filter would have dropped the collapsed bullet; reworded. Live run 7: one collapsed takeaway bullet, kernels 3/4 (one omitted), no repeated fallbacks.
_meta.v8_note: V8 (2026-09-11): owner-supplied rebuild replaces the source-free claim-analysis architecture (V4-V7.2) with research-first: lib/claimResearch.js runs a bounded Anthropic web_search pre-pass through groundedFacts (maxUses default 6 for this tool, 3 everywhere else), returns a structured evidence packet, and the synthesis call (no tools) may make empirical claims ONLY from the packet with source_ids validated in code. New response fields: analysis_mode='verified_research', research_status, researched_at, sources_examined[{id,title,publisher,url,date,source_type}] (pruned to sources actually cited), and source_ids[] on the_signal items / the_noise items / still_worth_verifying items. Cold cache: waits up to SIGNAL_RESEARCH_COLD_WAIT_MS then returns HTTP 503 code:research_unavailable rather than an unresearched answer — so a golden re-run can 503 on a cold server; run the case once to warm (24h TTL), then check. the_noise is now optional (items without a surviving source id drop). The regex/judge/rewrite/fallback machinery and CLAIM_MODE_FALLBACKS are gone; earlier DO-NOT notes in SIGNALVSNOISE-NOTES.md V4-V7.2 are superseded, not reversed. See the V8 section there for kit findings.
_meta.v8_3_note: V8.3 (2026-09-11): speed. (1) synthesis split into two parallel disjoint-key calls (signal+noise 3000 tok / verify+cant-decide+bottom-line+sources-of-noise 2200 tok) — same packet, different schema halves; (2) hard word caps per field in the prompt; (3) two-phase UX: new POST /signal-vs-noise/research returns immediately ({status:'pending', sources:[]} 202 while the fetch runs, {status:'ready', researched_at, claim_count, sources} once cached — starts the fetch on a cold topic; own rate-limit bucket 20/min), the client polls it every ~6s untracked (pollToolEndpoint), shows 'N sources found', then calls the main endpoint which finds the research cached and runs synthesis only. Main endpoint unchanged for direct callers (60s cold wait, 503). New golden case research-status-investing-warm checks the readiness shape; sources optional because a cold server answers pending.

input.conflictingAdvice: Index funds always win vs. active management can beat the market, time in market beats timing the market vs. valuations matter, real estate vs. stocks

still_worth_verifying.question: Does time in the market reliably beat timing the market across all investor horizons and starting valuations?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The two main claims directly conflict: staying invested is supported by illustrative analyses, but CAPE research suggests starting valuations shape long-run returns in ways those analyses do not address.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Controlled research comparing stay-invested strategies against valuation-aware tactical approaches across different CAPE starting points and time horizons

still_worth_verifying.question: Does real estate or stocks produce better net long-run returns for individual investors?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The answer shifts materially depending on whether rental income, leverage, maintenance costs, taxes, and transaction costs are included — and the sub-period studied changes the result substantially.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Standardized comparisons using individual-investor-level costs, leverage, and tax treatment across the same time periods; only secondary sources were found for this claim.

still_worth_verifying.question: Can genuinely active managers — measured by high active share — reliably outperform after costs in specific market niches?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: The index-always-wins claim rests on aggregate averages; whether a specific category of active management sustainably outperforms is a separate and unresolved question.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Post-publication replication of active share findings across longer periods and different cost environments

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether index or active funds fit your situation depends on which asset categories you hold, your tax circumstances, and the specific funds available to you — general averages do not resolve this.

Whether high current valuations should change your own investment behavior depends on your time horizon, risk tolerance, and whether you would successfully re-enter the market after exiting — the research does not answer that.

Whether real estate or stocks is better for you depends on your access to capital, ability to manage property, geographic market, tax situation, and need for liquidity — none of which the general evidence addresses.

supported_takeaways: Index funds outperform active funds on average across most equity and all bond categories studied, but actively managed small-cap and international funds outperformed their index over most of one study period — the 'always' framing is not supported. [S4, S5]

High starting valuations as measured by CAPE have historically predicted lower long-run S&P 500 returns over periods exceeding 10 years, and this relationship appeared across 17 international markets — though CAPE does not function as a short-term timing tool. [S10]

When total returns including rental income and dividends are counted, residential real estate and equities produced broadly similar inflation-adjusted long-run returns across 16 countries from 1870 to 2015 — though the 1980–2015 sub-period favored stocks by a wide margin. [S12, S13, S14]
treat_skeptically: 'Index funds always win' overstates the evidence — specific niches and time windows show active outperformance, and survivorship bias in aggregate data inflates the passive advantage. [S4, S5]

'Time in the market beats timing the market' as an absolute rule is supported only by illustrative secondary analyses, not controlled research, and does not account for valuation-adjusted expected returns. [S7, S8, S10]

Simple real-estate-versus-stocks comparisons that omit rental income, maintenance costs, leverage, and taxes are methodologically incomplete and can point in either direction depending on what is included or excluded. [S14]
what_would_change_the_answer: Peer-reviewed research directly comparing valuation-aware investment strategies against stay-invested strategies over matched time horizons would sharpen the time-in-market vs. valuations conflict.
Individual-level real estate return data accounting for actual costs, leverage, and taxes — rather than economy-wide aggregates — would make the real estate vs. stocks comparison more actionable.
Longer post-publication data on active share and performance persistence would clarify whether high-active-share outperformance holds after the finding became widely known.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A finding that holds on average across a large sample gets restated as a rule that holds always and for everyone, erasing the exceptions the original research documented.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Words like 'always,' 'never,' or 'always beats' where the cited evidence uses 'on average' or 'most.'

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Choosing a start and end date that flatters a particular asset class produces a compelling historical chart that does not generalize to other periods covered by the same underlying research.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A comparison that highlights one time window without acknowledging that a different window reverses the result.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Gross return figures — omitting fees, taxes, transaction costs, or maintenance — make one asset class appear superior to what net-return research would support.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: A return comparison that does not specify whether rental income, dividends, costs, or leverage are included.

output.topic_as_understood: Whether index funds reliably beat active management, whether staying invested beats market timing, and whether stocks or real estate produce better long-term returns
output.framing: Most of these debates collapse when you add the word 'always' or 'better' — the researched evidence supports narrower, conditional versions of each claim, not the universal ones.

items.claim: Index funds outperform most active funds on average, but not all categories in all periods
items.basis: A peer-reviewed study found index funds outperformed active funds across most equity and all bond categories on average; a separate Journal of Financial Economics study found that funds with higher 'active share' (genuinely active, not closet indexers) earned roughly 1% more per year in benchmark-adjusted returns — suggesting the average hides meaningful variation.
items.limits: The S4 study is from 2002; active-share research applies most clearly where passive alternatives are scarce. Survivorship bias inflates active funds' apparent failure rate.

items.claim: Starting valuations, measured by CAPE, have historically predicted long-run S&P 500 return ranges — not timing, but the general level of future returns
items.basis: A working paper found CAPE-based forecasts of 10-plus-year S&P 500 returns held up historically and also applied across 17 MSCI country indexes since 1979. This supports valuations as a long-horizon return signal, not a tactical exit trigger.
items.limits: CAPE predicts return ranges, not drawdown timing. High valuations can persist for years. The paper is an SSRN preprint, not yet a published journal study, and model outputs vary with specification.

the_noise.noise_label: Universal claim that ignores documented exceptions
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Index funds outperform most active funds on average over long periods; certain categories — small-cap equity, international funds, some bond niches — have shown active outperformance in documented research.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: 'Always' is flatly contradicted by the same peer-reviewed evidence used to support passive investing's general advantage.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: For broadly diversified equity categories over long horizons, the average active fund has underperformed its index after costs.

the_noise.claim: Time in the market beats timing the market — stated as a universal rule
the_noise.noise_label: True in general; incomplete against valuation-based objections
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Staying invested has historically outperformed attempting to exit and re-enter on short-term predictions; but CAPE research shows starting valuations do predict long-run return ranges, which the simple slogan does not address.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The slogan conflates short-term market-timing (hard to execute, well-documented to fail) with valuation-aware long-horizon positioning, which operates on different evidence.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Missing even a handful of the best market days substantially reduces long-run returns, making reactive exits costly.

the_noise.claim: Real estate is better than stocks (or vice versa) as a long-term investment
the_noise.noise_label: Comparison depends entirely on methodology and time period
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Over 145 years across 16 economies, total returns were similar when rental income and dividends are both counted; stocks led decisively in the 1980-2015 sub-period. Neither asset class is categorically superior across all periods studied.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The framing treats 'real estate vs. stocks' as a single answerable question, but the answer flips depending on whether rental income is included, which country and period is examined, and whether leverage and costs are counted.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Real estate's lower correlation with equities has historically improved risk-adjusted outcomes when both are held together in a portfolio.

input.conflictingAdvice: Indexfonds gewinnen immer vs. aktives Management kann den Markt schlagen, Zeit im Markt schlaegt Markt-Timing vs. Bewertungen sind wichtig

still_worth_verifying.question: Ob 'Zeit im Markt schlägt Timing' durch Langzeitdaten aus primärer Forschung direkt belegt ist
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Die Evidenz für diesen Claim stammt ausschließlich aus Sekundärquellen (S6, S7, S8) – kein peer-reviewtes Primärpapier im Paket.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Peer-reviewte Langzeitstudien zu Anlegerrenditen im Vergleich zu Buy-and-Hold-Strategien

still_worth_verifying.question: Gilt die Vorhersagekraft des Shiller-CAPE für deutsche oder Eurozone-Märkte eigenständig?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Das vorliegende CAPE-Papier basiert primär auf US- und internationalen MSCI-Daten; deutschlandspezifische Befunde fehlen.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Replikationsstudien zum CAPE für DAX oder MSCI Germany über vergleichbare Zeiträume

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Ob Indexfonds oder aktives Management für das konkrete Depot dieser Person – je nach Anlageklasse, Kosten und Zeithorizont – das bessere Ergebnis liefert

Wie lange der relevante Anlagehorizont sein muss, damit die Logik 'Zeit im Markt schlägt Timing' praktisch Gewicht erhält – die Forschung deutet auf 10+ Jahre, aber die konkrete Anwendung hängt von der individuellen Situation ab.

Ob ein bestimmtes CAPE-Niveau als aktuelles Marktrisiko interpretiert werden sollte – die Forschung bestätigt Vorhersagekraft über lange Zeiträume, sagt aber nicht, wie das aktuelle Niveau bewertungsfreundlich ist oder wie es in eine konkrete Anlagestrategie einfließt.

supported_takeaways: Die Mehrheit aktiv verwalteter europäischer Aktienfonds schnitt laut SPIVA Mid-Year 2025 schlechter ab als ihr Benchmark – und Top-Performer blieben das selten dauerhaft. [S4, S5]

Laut Morningstar und Bank of Singapore verdienen Anleger im Durchschnitt weniger pro investiertem Dollar, als die Fonds selbst erwirtschaften – ein Muster, das mit häufigen Ein- und Ausstiegsversuchen assoziiert ist, aber durch sekundäre Quellen gestützt wird. [S6, S8]
Das Shiller-CAPE zeigt laut einem SSRN-Preprint einen Zusammenhang mit langfristigen Aktienrenditen über 10+ Jahre, eignet sich aber nicht als kurzfristiges Timing-Werkzeug. [S9]
treat_skeptically: 'Indexfonds gewinnen immer' – kurzfristig und in Teilsegmenten gibt es Ausnahmen; die Aussage ist zu absolut. [S4, S5]
'Bewertungen sind wichtig' als Argument für kurzfristiges Market-Timing – das CAPE-Papier belegt Vorhersagekraft nur auf 10+-Jahreshorizont, nicht für Einstiegszeitpunkte. [S9]
what_would_change_the_answer: Primärforschung zur 'Zeit im Markt'-These würde den Evidenzgrad erheblich stärken oder einschränken
Eigenständige CAPE-Studien für Deutschland oder die Eurozone würden die Relevanz für hiesige Anleger klären

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Aus 'gilt statistisch für die Mehrheit über lange Zeiträume' wird 'gilt immer' – Ausnahmen und Bedingungen fallen weg.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Formulierungen ohne Zeitrahmen, Bedingung oder Ausnahme

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Langfristige Bewertungszusammenhänge (10+ Jahre) werden als Argument für kurzfristige Ein- oder Ausstiegsentscheidungen verwendet.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: CAPE oder ähnliche Kennzahlen als Timing-Signal statt als Erwartungsrahmen

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Aktive Fonds oder Markttimer, die erfolgreich waren, werden sichtbar; die Mehrheit der Misserfolge verschwindet aus der Wahrnehmung.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Einzelbeispiele erfolgreicher Manager ohne Vergleich zur Gesamtheit aller Manager

output.topic_as_understood: Drei zentrale Investitionsthesen im Vergleich: Indexfonds vs. aktives Management, Zeit im Markt vs. Markt-Timing, und ob Bewertungskennzahlen wie das Shiller-CAPE zukünftige Renditen vorhersagen.
output.framing: Die drei Aussagen vermischen unterschiedliche Zeithorizonte und Anwendungsfelder – was als Faustregel gilt, stimmt selten als absolute Regel. Entscheidend ist, für welchen Zeitraum, welchen Markt und welchen Zweck eine Aussage gemacht wird.

items.claim: Aktiv verwaltete Fonds schneiden mehrheitlich schlechter ab als ihr Vergleichsindex – und das über längere Zeiträume konsistent.
items.basis: Der SPIVA Europe Mid-Year 2025-Datensatz von S&P Dow Jones Indices zeigt, dass 61 % der europäischen Aktienfonds und 59 % der Rentenfonds ihren Benchmark nicht erreichten. Ein weiterer S&P-Datensatz zur Persistenz zeigt: Kein einziger Top-Quartil-Large-Cap-Fonds von 2021 blieb über vier Jahre im Top-Quartil.
items.limits: In einzelnen Marktsegmenten oder Jahren können aktive Manager vorübergehend outperformen; die Daten sind für den deutschen Einzelfondsmarkt weniger detailliert.

items.claim: Das Shiller-CAPE hat nachgewiesene Vorhersagekraft für langfristige Marktrenditen – aber nur über sehr lange Zeiträume und mit erheblicher Unsicherheit.
items.basis: Ein auf SSRN veröffentlichter Preprint von Norbert Keimling zeigt einen statistischen Zusammenhang zwischen dem Shiller-CAPE und künftigen Renditen des S&P 500 über Zeiträume von mehr als 10 Jahren; der Autor berichtet eine Replikation über 17 MSCI-Länderindizes, jedoch ist diese Replikation selbst nicht durch separate peer-reviewte Primärquellen im Forschungspaket bestätigt.
items.limits: Die Vorhersagefehler betragen je nach Studie 1–3 Prozentpunkte p.a.; Änderungen bei Rechnungslegung und Aktienrückkäufen können den historischen Vergleich verzerren. Für Deutschland oder die Eurozone ist die eigenständige Evidenzlage dünner.

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Die Mehrheit aktiver Fonds bleibt über lange Zeiträume hinter ihrem Benchmark zurück; ob Indexfonds 'immer' gewinnen, ist nicht belegt – kurzfristig und in einzelnen Segmenten zeigt die Datenlage Ausnahmen.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Das Wort 'immer' schließt keine Ausnahmen ein. Die SPIVA-Daten zeigen eine Mehrheit, keine Vollständigkeit – und betreffen bestimmte Fondstypen und Zeiträume.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Über längere Zeiträume schneiden die meisten aktiven Fonds nach Kosten schlechter ab als ihr Index.

the_noise.claim: Bewertungen sind wichtig (impliziert: CAPE eignet sich für Markt-Timing)
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Bewertungskennzahlen wie das CAPE sind sinnvoll für die Einschätzung langfristiger Renditeerwartungen und die strategische Vermögensaufteilung – nicht für kurzfristiges Ein- und Aussteigen.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Die populäre Lesart vermischt die nachgewiesene Langfrist-Vorhersagekraft des CAPE mit der Idee, damit Marktein- und -ausstiege zu steuern. Das ist durch die Evidenz nicht gedeckt.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Das CAPE hat über Zeithorizonte von mehr als 10 Jahren statistisch nachweisbare Vorhersagekraft für Marktrenditen.

input.conflictingAdvice: Screen time is destroying kids vs. it depends on content, tiger parenting vs. free-range, homework helps vs. homework is harmful

still_worth_verifying.question: Does screen time affect adolescents differently than young children, and do the same content and context moderators apply?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Most screen time research is concentrated in early childhood; whether findings extend to teens is not established by the packet.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Longitudinal studies tracking outcomes by age group and content type into adolescence would clarify this.

still_worth_verifying.question: Do the harms of heavy homework — stress, lost family time, equity effects — outweigh achievement gains at secondary level?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Meta-analyses focus on achievement; non-achievement costs are rarely measured, leaving the net-benefit question open.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies that measure both achievement and wellbeing outcomes together, with consistent quantity and quality controls.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does parental warmth within a demanding parenting style consistently moderate child outcomes across cultures outside East Asian and Asian American samples?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: If warmth is the key variable, the tiger vs. free-range framing may be a distraction; but the evidence base is narrow.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Comparative longitudinal studies across diverse cultural contexts using consistent definitions of warmth and demandingness.

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether a specific child's screen use is harming them depends on content, co-use, timing, and what the screen time displaces — none of which general population findings can determine for one family.

Whether a demanding parenting approach will help or harm a specific child depends on how much warmth accompanies it, the child's temperament, and cultural context — variables the general evidence notes but cannot resolve for an individual.

Whether homework is worth assigning to a particular elementary-age child is not answered by the evidence, which finds near-zero average achievement correlation at that level while leaving individual variation unexamined.

supported_takeaways: For screen time, content and context — co-use, age-appropriateness, timing — are associated with meaningfully different outcomes, so a simple hours-per-day rule is less precise than what the evidence suggests matters. [S1, S4]

For homework, grade level is the most robust moderator: the case for homework is substantially weaker at elementary level than at high school, where one meta-analysis found a meaningful achievement advantage for students who did homework. [S8, S10]

For demanding parenting, the presence or absence of warmth alongside strictness is associated with different child outcomes; purely power-assertive profiles were not clearly dominant even in Asian American samples where tiger parenting is most studied. [S6, S7]
treat_skeptically: 'Screen time is destroying kids' — the packet finds associations with some harms but cannot establish causality, and co-use and educational content show positive associations. [S1, S3]
'Tiger parenting produces superior outcomes' — a longitudinal study found it associated with lower GPA and more depressive symptoms compared with a supportive profile. [S5, S7]
'Homework helps' as a universal claim — the achievement benefit at elementary level was near zero in the landmark meta-analysis; the claim holds better at high school. [S8, S10]
what_would_change_the_answer: Experimental or quasi-experimental designs on screen time that can separate content type, duration, and displacement effects would sharpen the evidence considerably.
Homework research that measures stress, equity, and family outcomes alongside achievement would allow a genuine net-benefit assessment.
Parenting style research across more diverse cultural contexts with consistent definitions of warmth and demandingness would clarify how generalizable the existing findings are.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Associations in population studies get reported as 'X causes harm,' making findings sound more definitive than the designs support.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Look for 'causes' or 'destroys' where the study was observational.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A finding about average outcomes across a sample gets stated as a rule for every child, dropping moderators like age, content, or warmth.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Claims with no age, context, or condition qualifier attached.

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Parenting and screen debates get cast as either/or opposites when the evidence shows outcomes depend on combinations of variables, not a single dimension.
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Headlines framed as 'X vs. Y' with no room for 'it depends on Z.'

output.topic_as_understood: Whether screen time, strict/tiger parenting, and homework help or harm children, based on available research
output.framing: All three debates share the same underlying problem: flat yes/no claims are being made about outcomes that the cited evidence indicates depend on age, context, and conditions. The research supports nuance, not blanket verdicts.

items.claim: Screen time effects depend meaningfully on content, timing, and whether a parent watches with the child — not just total hours.
items.basis: A 2024 meta-analysis in JAMA Pediatrics found that co-viewing was positively associated with cognitive outcomes, while background TV and age-inappropriate content were associated with worse outcomes. A separate 2025 prospective study associated high screen time with lower elementary academic achievement, but could not establish causation.
items.limits: Most studies are observational; causality not established. Research is concentrated in early childhood.

items.claim: For homework, grade level is the most reliable moderator: the achievement link is near zero for elementary students, modest for middle schoolers, and more meaningful for high schoolers.
items.basis: Cooper et al.'s meta-analysis found correlations of approximately zero (elementary), r = .07 (middle school), and r = .25 (high school). A 2017 meta-analysis found a small overall effect (d = 0.229) across all levels, and a 2026 meta-analysis of digital homework found a similar modest positive effect (g = 0.309).
items.limits: Correlational designs dominate; reverse causality is plausible. Potential harms — stress, equity effects — are underrepresented in these analyses.

items.claim: Tiger parenting is not one thing, and the outcomes depend heavily on whether strictness is paired with warmth.
items.basis: A longitudinal study of 400+ Chinese American families found tiger parenting associated with lower GPA and more depressive symptoms than supportive parenting. An APA Division 7 review of six studies found that parental warmth moderates outcomes, and that purely power-assertive parenting was not actually the dominant profile in the cultures studied.
items.limits: Research is concentrated in East Asian and Asian American samples; generalizability to other cultural contexts is limited.

the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: High screen time is associated with some worse outcomes, but co-viewing and educational content show neutral or positive associations — 'destroying' overstates a conditional, correlational finding.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The wording implies universal, causal harm. The evidence is observational, shows moderated effects, and finds some screen contexts associated with better outcomes.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Heavy background TV and age-inappropriate content are associated with worse cognitive and psychosocial outcomes.

the_noise.claim: Tiger parenting produces superior child outcomes.
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Authoritative parenting — high in both demands and warmth — is associated with better outcomes than purely strict profiles. Tiger parenting outcomes vary with the presence of parental warmth.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: The claim strips out the warmth variable that the evidence identifies as a key moderator, and generalizes from one cultural context to all children.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: High parental expectations are not inherently harmful; warmth alongside them changes the outcome picture substantially.

the_noise.claim: Homework helps academic achievement (implied as universal).
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: The achievement benefit of homework is near zero for elementary students, modest in middle school, and more meaningful in high school. The universal claim is not supported.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Aggregating across age groups obscures the grade-level moderator, which is the most consistent finding in the meta-analytic literature.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: For high school students, homework is associated with meaningfully better achievement compared to no homework.

input.topic: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
input.conflictingAdvice: My coworker says blue light glasses fixed her insomnia. Another friend says sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends, but my doctor said catching up on weekends helps.

still_worth_verifying.question: Does weekend catch-up sleep help or harm over the long term?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Both the friend and doctor are partially right; the disagreement reflects genuine scientific uncertainty, not a clear answer.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Long-term experimental studies tracking metabolic and cognitive outcomes across years of sustained catch-up patterns

still_worth_verifying.question: Do commercially sold blue-light glasses with low filter strength improve sleep?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: Most trials tested high-filter amber lenses worn 2+ hours before bed — not the glasses most people actually buy and use.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: RCTs specifically testing low-filter lenses worn during the day, the most common real-world use case

still_worth_verifying.question: How large a weekly sleep deficit makes weekend catch-up meaningfully insufficient?
still_worth_verifying.why_it_matters: A small nightly shortfall and a large one are different problems, but research does not consistently specify thresholds.
still_worth_verifying.what_would_help: Studies that define and compare deficit magnitude rather than treating any short sleep as equivalent

what_general_claims_cant_decide: Whether the coworker's insomnia improvement came from blue-light reduction, a placebo effect, or a behavioral change that happened alongside wearing the glasses
What your personal optimal sleep duration is — the recommended range reflects individual variation, and population findings cannot specify it for one person

Whether weekend catch-up is advisable for you depends on how large your weekly deficit is, how irregular your schedule becomes, and what symptom you are trying to address — none of which the general evidence resolves

supported_takeaways: The professional consensus from NSF, AASM, and CDC is 7–9 hours for most adults, not a fixed 8 — individual need varies within that range [S1, S2, S3]

Weekend catch-up sleep may partially restore mood and reduce fatigue short-term, but available evidence suggests it cannot fully offset chronic restriction and may introduce circadian disruption [S10, S12]

Blue-light blocking glasses show inconsistent results across trials — subjective sleep improvement has been reported in some RCTs, but objective actigraphy measures across studies have not shown significant change [S6, S7, S9]
treat_skeptically: 'Exactly 8 hours' as a universal requirement — authoritative bodies explicitly frame the recommendation as a range, not a fixed number [S1, S3]
The claim that blue-light glasses 'fixed' insomnia — the most rigorous pooled analysis found no significant objective sleep improvement, and placebo effects cannot be ruled out [S6]

Both the flat claim that sleep debt cannot be repaid and the flat claim that weekend catch-up helps — the evidence supports neither fully and shows the two effects work against each other [S10, S11, S12]
what_would_change_the_answer: Larger, longer-term RCTs on blue-light glasses testing the specific lens types people actually use
Experimental studies tracking health outcomes of sustained weekly catch-up patterns over months or years, not just short-term studies

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A range recommendation gets collapsed into one memorable figure, making it feel like a universal rule rather than a population guideline with individual variation
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: No qualifier like 'most adults' or 'on average' appears alongside the specific number

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: A genuine individual improvement becomes a universal recommendation, ignoring that the cause may not transfer to others with different insomnia triggers
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: The claim is stated as a fix rather than 'this worked for me'

sources_of_noise.how_it_distorts: Feeling better after a product or behavior gets reported as the product working, even when measured outcomes do not match self-reported ones
sources_of_noise.how_to_recognize_it: Evidence cited is self-report or anecdote, with no mention of whether objective measures agreed

output.topic_as_understood: Whether adults need exactly 8 hours of sleep, whether blue light glasses reliably fix insomnia, and whether weekend sleep can repay a weekly sleep deficit
output.framing: All three claims contain a real finding but overstate its precision or universality. The evidence supports ranges and partial effects, not fixed rules or definitive fixes.

items.claim: Healthy adult sleep need falls in a range — roughly 7 to 9 hours — not a fixed 8 hours
items.basis: The NSF, AASM, Sleep Research Society, and CDC all recommend a range for adults. Epidemiological data associate both short sleep (<6 hrs) and long sleep (9+ hrs) with poorer cardiovascular health and higher depression rates, suggesting a U-shaped relationship rather than a single optimal number.
items.limits: Large studies rely on self-reported duration; causality — whether short sleep causes harm or illness causes short sleep — is hard to establish from observational data.

items.claim: Weekend catch-up sleep appears to offer partial short-term relief but does not fully reverse chronic sleep debt, and irregular timing may add its own costs
items.basis: A 2025 systematic review found catch-up sleep can restore some mood, reduce fatigue, and partially recover cognitive performance, but not fully offset chronic deprivation. A 2025 paper on sleep homeostasis identifies a paradox: extra weekend duration may aid recovery while the timing shift simultaneously causes circadian misalignment.
items.limits: Most studies are observational or short-term experiments. Long-term consequences of a sustained weekly catch-up pattern are not well characterized. The size of the nightly deficit likely matters but thresholds are not consistently defined.

the_noise.claim: Everyone needs exactly 8 hours of sleep or their health suffers
the_noise.noise_label: False precision on a real range
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Most adults need somewhere between 7 and 9 hours; individual need varies, and both too little and too much are associated with poorer health outcomes.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: 'Exactly 8' collapses a recommended range into one number and implies any deviation causes harm, which the evidence does not support.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Consistently short sleep is genuinely associated with health risks — the concern is real, just not pinned to a single number.

the_noise.claim: Blue light glasses fixed her insomnia
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Some individuals report better sleep quality with blue-blocking glasses; objective actigraphy measures show inconsistent or non-significant effects across trials. At best, they may help when evening screen exposure is a contributing factor.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: A personal experience of improvement cannot rule out placebo or behavioral change. The most rigorous pooled analysis found no significant objective effect on sleep onset or total sleep time.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Some RCTs do find subjective sleep quality improvements, particularly with high-filter amber lenses worn 2+ hours before bed.

the_noise.claim: Sleep debt cannot be repaid on weekends (absolute version) vs. catching up on weekends fully helps (absolute version)
the_noise.noise_label: Both absolutes overstate a genuinely mixed picture
the_noise.what_the_evidence_supports_instead: Weekend catch-up sleep provides real but partial short-term recovery. Whether it helps or harms overall depends on how large the deficit is and how much the schedule shift disrupts circadian timing.
the_noise.what_went_wrong: Both positions pick one side of evidence that points in two directions simultaneously. Neither accounts for the trade-off between homeostatic recovery and circadian disruption.
the_noise.kernel_of_truth: Your friend is right that full biological recovery from chronic restriction is not established. Your doctor is right that some measurable recovery does occur.
